claims.text: Machine-learning-accelerated thermodynamic integration can substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties without sacrificing free-energy fidelity.
Relevant elemental and binary systems have previously been studied using explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
A strategically small ab initio molecular-dynamics dataset can adequately cover the important temperature and structural regimes needed to train the MLIPs.
MLIP-based thermodynamic integration can compute the free energies of both solid and liquid phases.
An interatomic-potential workflow can be extended to quinary high-entropy alloys.
The proposed scope extends from temperatures near melting to lower elevated temperatures where phase free-energy differences are important.
The MLIPs can capture vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects needed for accurate free-energy calculations.
The MLIPs can capture electron–vibration interactions needed for accurate free-energy calculations.
Training on a limited set of high-fidelity ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations will accurately reproduce the relevant potential-energy surface.
Reproducing the potential-energy surface with an MLIP enables high-throughput thermodynamic integration while avoiding the extensive sampling cost of full ab initio molecular dynamics.
MLIP acceleration will preserve the key entropy contributions and phase free energies.
The workflow will reduce simulation cost by roughly one order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The workflow will reproduce reference free energies within approximately 5% deviation.
The workflow will have fidelity similar or superior to TOR-TILD, especially for multicomponent systems.
TOR-TILD slows substantially when applied to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The efficiency gains for extremely disordered high-entropy alloys have not yet been quantitatively demonstrated.

The decisive benchmark will compare solid and liquid free energies, melting temperature, vibrational entropy, and anharmonic free-energy contributions against full ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD for the same system.
The hypothesis is falsified if deviations exceed 5% or if the speedup relative to TOR-TILD is less than one order of magnitude in either elemental/binary or multicomponent tests.
